questions.stem: The central nervous system consists of:
options: the brain and spinal cord
the brain and cranial nerves
the spinal cord and skeletal muscles
the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves
questions.explanation: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. All the nerves outside them, including the somatic and autonomic systems, form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: A student decides to raise her hand to answer a question. Which division of the nervous system carries the message to the muscles of her arm?
options: the autonomic nervous system
the parasympathetic nervous system
the sympathetic nervous system
the somatic nervous system
questions.explanation: The somatic nervous system carries sensory information to the CNS and motor messages to skeletal muscles for voluntary movement. The autonomic system controls involuntary functions such as heart rate.

questions.stem: Which function is controlled by the autonomic nervous system?
options: regulating heart rate and digestion
kicking a football towards a goal
feeling the texture of sandpaper
writing an answer on a test paper
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary activity of internal organs and glands. Kicking and writing are voluntary movements, and touch sensations travel through the somatic system.

questions.stem: After a near miss on the road, a driver's heart pounds and her breathing quickens. A few minutes later her heart rate returns to normal. Which divisions are responsible, in order?
options: parasympathetic, then sympathetic
somatic, then autonomic
central, then peripheral
sympathetic, then parasympathetic
questions.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system arouses the body in response to threat. The parasympathetic nervous system then calms the body and restores normal functioning.

questions.stem: In Parkinson's disease, neurons that produce dopamine are lost, and people develop tremors and slow, stiff movement. What does this show about the nervous system?
options: Damage to brain chemicals can disrupt voluntary movement
Movement is controlled only by the peripheral nervous system
Dopamine is involved only in reward and not in movement
The parasympathetic system controls all voluntary movement
questions.explanation: Dopamine-producing neurons in the brain help coordinate smooth voluntary movement. Their loss shows how a compromised part of the CNS affects behaviour, even though the muscles and nerves are healthy.

questions.stem: Which type of neuron carries messages from the senses towards the central nervous system?
options: interneurons
mirror neurons
sensory neurons
motor neurons
questions.explanation: Sensory, or afferent, neurons carry information from receptors to the CNS. Motor neurons carry messages from the CNS to muscles and glands.

questions.stem: Interneurons are best described as neurons that:
options: carry information from receptors in the skin to the spinal cord
release hormones directly into the bloodstream to reach organs
connect sensory and motor neurons within the central nervous system
carry messages from the spinal cord to muscles in the arms and legs
questions.explanation: Interneurons are found only in the brain and spinal cord, where they relay and integrate messages between sensory and motor neurons.

questions.stem: A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away. In order, which neurons are involved?
options: sensory, then motor, then interneurons
sensory, then interneurons, then motor
motor, then interneurons, then sensory
interneurons, then sensory, then motor
questions.explanation: Sensory neurons carry the heat signal to the spinal cord, interneurons relay it, and motor neurons carry the message to the arm muscles to withdraw the hand.

questions.stem: What is the function of the myelin sheath?
options: It speeds up transmission of messages along the axon
It receives messages from neighbouring neurons
It releases neurotransmitters into the synapse
It stores memories within the neuron's cell body
questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, so neural impulses travel faster. Dendrites receive messages and axon terminals release neurotransmitters.

questions.stem: Which lobe is mainly responsible for processing visual information?
options: the frontal lobe
the occipital lobe
the temporal lobe
the parietal lobe
questions.explanation: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, contains the primary visual cortex. The temporal lobe processes sound, the parietal lobe touch and spatial information, and the frontal lobe planning and movement.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a man can no longer feel touch on his left arm, although he can still move it. Which lobe is most likely damaged?
options: the left parietal lobe
the right occipital lobe
the left frontal lobe
the right parietal lobe
questions.explanation: The somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe receives touch sensations, and each hemisphere receives input from the opposite side of the body. Movement is controlled by the frontal lobe, which seems unaffected.

questions.stem: Which lobe contains the primary auditory cortex and plays a role in understanding speech?
options: the parietal lobe
the frontal lobe
the temporal lobe
the occipital lobe
questions.explanation: The temporal lobe processes sounds and contains Wernicke's area, involved in understanding language. It also has a role in memory.

questions.stem: A person has difficulty planning, controlling impulses and starting voluntary movements. Which lobe is most likely affected?
options: the temporal lobe
the parietal lobe
the frontal lobe
the occipital lobe
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe contains the prefrontal cortex, which supports planning and impulse control, and the primary motor cortex, which initiates voluntary movement.

questions.stem: The prefrontal cortex is mainly involved in:
options: regulating heartbeat and breathing automatically
forming fear memories of threatening events
planning, decision-making and controlling impulses
processing visual information from the eyes
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex carries out executive functions such as planning, reasoning, judgement and inhibiting impulses. Fear responses involve the amygdala.

questions.stem: In 1848 a railway worker, Phineas Gage, survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe. Reports describe him as more impulsive and less reliable afterwards. Which structure's role does this case illustrate?
options: the hippocampus
the occipital lobe
the cerebellum
the prefrontal cortex
questions.explanation: Damage to the prefrontal cortex can change personality, judgement and impulse control. Gage's case is often used to show this, though accounts of the changes vary in detail.

questions.stem: A patient who had surgery to remove parts of both hippocampi could still remember his childhood but could not form new long-term memories of events. What does this suggest about the hippocampus?
options: It is essential for forming new explicit memories
It is the place where all old memories are stored
It controls voluntary movement of the body
It processes visual information from the eyes
questions.explanation: This pattern, seen in Henry Molaison, shows the hippocampus is needed to consolidate new explicit memories but not to retrieve older ones, which are stored elsewhere in the cortex.

questions.stem: Which structure is most involved in detecting threats and producing fear responses?
options: the occipital lobe
the prefrontal cortex
the amygdala
the hippocampus
questions.explanation: The amygdala rapidly evaluates stimuli for threat and triggers fear responses. The prefrontal cortex can help regulate these responses.

questions.stem: Brain imaging of people with an anxiety disorder often shows an overactive amygdala and reduced regulation from the prefrontal cortex. Which explanation of their symptoms fits this?
options: Voluntary movements cannot be started by the motor cortex
Threat responses are stronger and less well controlled
Visual information is processed more slowly than usual
New memories cannot be formed at all in the hippocampus
questions.explanation: An overactive amygdala signals threat too readily, and weaker prefrontal control makes it harder to calm the response, contributing to excessive worry and fear.

questions.stem: Which statement about exercise and the brain is best supported by research?
options: Regular aerobic exercise is linked to better memory and mood
Exercise affects only the muscles and has no link with brain function
Exercise reduces the number of neurons in the hippocampus over time
Exercise improves brain function only in people under the age of 20
questions.explanation: Aerobic exercise increases blood flow and growth factors in the brain and is linked to improved memory and mood. Benefits have been found across the lifespan, including older adults.

questions.stem: How can prolonged trauma or chronic stress affect the brain?
options: Stress hormones improve memory more the longer they stay high
Long-term high cortisol can harm the hippocampus
Chronic stress increases the size of the prefrontal cortex in every person
Trauma affects only physical health and leaves the brain unchanged
questions.explanation: Prolonged release of cortisol is linked to reduced hippocampal volume and a more reactive amygdala. This may help explain memory and emotional difficulties after trauma, such as in PTSD.

questions.stem: Children growing up in poverty, on average, show differences in brain development compared with wealthier peers. Which explanation is most consistent with a biopsychosocial view?
options: The brain is fixed at birth, so these differences must be inherited
Children in poverty choose not to use their brains as much as others
Stress, poor nutrition and fewer learning chances can play a part
Poverty changes a child's genes so the brain cannot develop normally
questions.explanation: Poverty brings stressors, poorer nutrition and fewer enriching experiences, which can affect brain development. Because the brain is plastic, supportive interventions can reduce these effects.

questions.stem: Social media apps give unpredictable rewards such as likes. Which neurotransmitter is most associated with this reward-based learning?
options: dopamine
cortisol
oxytocin
melatonin
questions.explanation: Dopamine is released in reward pathways when we receive or anticipate rewards, which strengthens the behaviours that led to them. This helps explain why checking social media can become habitual.

questions.stem: The nucleus accumbens, part of the brain's reward circuit, is often studied in research on addiction. Why?
options: It processes all sounds that enter through the ears
Addictive drugs and behaviours raise dopamine activity there
It is where long-term memories of facts are permanently stored
It controls voluntary movement of the arms and legs
questions.explanation: Drugs and some behaviours raise dopamine in reward circuits including the nucleus accumbens, reinforcing the behaviour. Repeated activation is thought to contribute to compulsive use.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a neurotransmitter and a hormone?
options: Neurotransmitters cross synapses; hormones travel in the bloodstream
Hormones cross synapses; neurotransmitters travel in the bloodstream
Neurotransmitters act slowly; hormones act within milliseconds
Hormones are made only in the brain; neurotransmitters only in glands
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are released by neurons and act quickly across the synapse. Hormones are released by glands into the blood and act more slowly on distant targets.

questions.stem: Which chemical is released by the adrenal glands during stress and helps mobilise energy?
options: dopamine
cortisol
serotonin
oxytocin
questions.explanation: Cortisol is a stress hormone that raises blood glucose and helps the body cope with ongoing stress. Prolonged high levels can harm health.

questions.stem: Oxytocin is most associated with:
options: the body's response to long-term stress
coordinating smooth voluntary movement
regulating sleep and the body clock
social bonding, trust and attachment
questions.explanation: Oxytocin, released in situations such as childbirth, breastfeeding and close contact, promotes bonding and trust. Cortisol is linked to stress and dopamine to movement and reward.

questions.stem: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter mainly linked to:
options: release of adrenaline
visual processing in the eyes
mood, sleep and appetite
muscle contraction in the legs
questions.explanation: Serotonin helps regulate mood, sleep and appetite. Low serotonin activity has been linked to depression, which is why many antidepressants target it.

questions.stem: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are commonly used to treat depression. How do they work?
options: They destroy neurons that produce excess serotonin
They block all neurotransmitters from crossing synapses
They replace serotonin with the hormone cortisol
They keep more serotonin available in the synapse
questions.explanation: SSRIs slow the reabsorption of serotonin by the sending neuron, so more remains in the synapse to act on receiving neurons. They are a biologically based treatment.

questions.stem: Which statement about the biological basis of depression is most accurate?
options: Depression results from damage to the occipital lobe in every case
Biology contributes, but psychological and social factors matter too
Depression is caused only by low serotonin, so medication always cures it
Depression has no biological basis and is caused only by life events
questions.explanation: Depression is associated with changes in neurotransmitters, stress hormones and the functioning of areas such as the prefrontal cortex and amygdala. However, it arises from interacting biological, psychological and social factors.

questions.stem: Some people with depression show reduced prefrontal cortex activity. Which symptom could this help explain?
options: loss of feeling in the hands and feet
an inability to see objects on one side
tremors and stiffness in the arms
difficulty concentrating and making decisions
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex supports concentration, planning and decision-making, which are often impaired in depression. Tremors and stiffness are associated with Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: Optogenetics is an experimental technique being researched as a possible treatment for depression and Parkinson's disease. What does it involve?
options: Passing a strong electric current through the brain to cause a seizure
Holding a magnetic coil over the scalp to stimulate the cortex
Prescribing medication that increases serotonin in synapses
Genetically altering neurons so that light controls their activity
questions.explanation: Optogenetics inserts light-sensitive proteins into specific neurons so researchers can switch them on or off with light. It has mainly been used in animal research, which raises ethical questions about its use in humans.

questions.stem: Which is the main ethical concern with developing an experimental brain treatment such as optogenetics for humans?
options: It is too cheap, so it could be overused in hospitals
It has already been proven safe in large human trials
It cannot be studied without the use of questionnaires
Unknown long-term risks of altering the brain
questions.explanation: Experimental treatments that alter brain tissue may have unknown or irreversible effects. Participants must give fully informed consent, and the potential benefits must justify the risks.

questions.stem: Why can it be difficult to gain informed consent from participants with brain injuries?
options: Brain injury research never involves any risk to participants
Consent is never needed when research is carried out in hospitals
Their injury may affect their ability to understand the research
People with brain injuries are not allowed to take part in research
questions.explanation: Damage to areas involved in memory, reasoning or language can impair a person's capacity to understand what they are agreeing to. Researchers may need consent from a guardian and must still respect the person's wishes.

questions.stem: A video game company funds research into which brain responses keep players engaged, so it can design games that are harder to stop playing. Why is this ethically problematic?
options: The research would require players to undergo brain surgery
The findings could be used to exploit players' reward systems
Research on the brain cannot be funded by private companies
Video games have no effect on any brain chemicals
questions.explanation: Using knowledge of dopamine and reward to encourage compulsive play may harm wellbeing for commercial gain. Applying neuropsychology findings raises questions about manipulation and responsibility.

questions.stem: Much early neuropsychology research on brain structures was carried out on animals. Which is an ethical requirement for such research today?
options: Animals must give informed consent before any procedure is carried out
Animals may be used only if the research has already been done on humans
Animal research is acceptable only when no results are published
Pain and distress must be minimised and justified by the benefits
questions.explanation: Animal research must be justified by its likely benefits, use as few animals as possible and minimise pain and distress. Animals cannot consent, so their welfare must be protected by others.

questions.stem: Case studies of people with brain damage, such as Phineas Gage, have taught psychologists a great deal. What is their main limitation?
options: Findings from one unusual case may not generalise to others
Case studies always use very large, random samples
Case studies provide only numerical data from experiments
Case studies allow cause and effect to be established exactly
questions.explanation: Case studies give rich detail, but each case is unique, the damage is not controlled, and records may be incomplete, so conclusions may not apply to other people.
